md: A silver ring tarnishes. A cut apple browns. An iron gate flakes orange. All three are the same kind of change, and so is nearly every reaction that gets a metal out of the ground. Chemists call the family **redox**, and it rests on one idea: something is given away, and something else takes it.

prompt: Copper oxide is heated in a stream of hydrogen. Which of the two ends up with the oxygen?
explain: The hydrogen collects the oxygen and becomes water. The next section gives that event its proper name.

text: 1. Oxidation and reduction, in terms of oxygen

alt: A three-row table: oxidation gains oxygen, loses hydrogen and loses electrons, while reduction loses oxygen, gains hydrogen and gains electrons.
svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 302" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="coilt"><title id="coilt">A table of the three ways oxidation and reduction are defined: oxygen gained or lost, hydrogen lost or gained, and electrons lost or gained</title><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.4"><path d="M50 54 H640"/><path d="M50 96 H640"/><path d="M50 138 H640"/><path d="M50 180 H640"/><path d="M50 222 H640"/><path d="M50 54 V222"/><path d="M280 54 V222"/><path d="M460 54 V222"/><path d="M640 54 V222"/></g><g font-family="inherit" font-size="13" fill="currentColor"><text x="62" y="82" font-weight="600">What changes</text><text x="292" y="82" font-weight="600">Oxidation</text><text x="472" y="82" font-weight="600">Reduction</text><text x="62" y="124">oxygen</text><text x="292" y="124">gained</text><text x="472" y="124">lost</text><text x="62" y="166">hydrogen</text><text x="292" y="166">lost</text><text x="472" y="166">gained</text><text x="62" y="208">electrons (Higher Tier)</text><text x="292" y="208">lost</text><text x="472" y="208">gained</text><text x="50" y="36" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Three ways to spot oxidation and reduction</text><text x="50" y="56" font-size="11.5">Read a row across: what oxidation does to that thing, reduction does the opposite.</text><text x="50" y="256" font-size="12">OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss of electrons, Reduction Is Gain of electrons.</text><text x="50" y="280" font-size="12">Both happen together in the same reaction, which is why it is called redox.</text></g></svg>
caption: Read a row across: whatever oxidation does, reduction does the opposite.

md: **Oxidation is gaining oxygen. Reduction is losing it.** In $\ce{CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O}$ the copper oxide loses its oxygen, so it is **reduced**; the hydrogen gains it, so it is **oxidised**. Both happen at once, and that pairing is what **redox** is short for.

title: Why the two always travel together
md: Oxygen does not vanish; it moves. The moment one substance loses it, another has gained it. The same goes for hydrogen, and later for electrons. So an answer that names only half of what happened is only half an answer — which is why a question asks **which** substance was oxidised and **which** was reduced.

explain: Oxidation. Its partner, losing oxygen, is reduction — and in any one reaction both are happening.

the lower one is the same oxygen arriving.</text></g></svg>
caption: Read the same picture the other way: the hydrogen is losing hydrogen atoms to water.

md: Some reactions move hydrogen rather than oxygen, so the definitions have a second form. **Losing hydrogen is oxidation; gaining hydrogen is reduction.** It is the mirror image of the oxygen rule, which is easy to get backwards — so learn the table above as a whole, one row at a time, rather than as four separate facts.

prompt: A substance gains hydrogen during a reaction. What has happened to it?
explain: Gaining hydrogen is reduction, the mirror of gaining oxygen being oxidation.

md:
At Higher Tier the definitions go one level deeper, to **electrons**: **Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain** — **OIL RIG**.
Drop magnesium into copper(II) sulfate solution and each magnesium atom hands two electrons to a copper(II) ion. The magnesium **loses** electrons, so it is oxidised. The copper(II) ion **gains** them, so it is reduced. No oxygen is anywhere in the reaction, yet it is still redox.

prompt: OIL RIG: oxidation is ______ of electrons.
explain: Loss. Reduction is gain — which feels backwards, because a positive charge going up looks like an increase.

Check: 0 on the left, +3 and −3 on the right</text><text x="392" y="214" font-size="13.5" font-weight="600">balanced</text><text x="40" y="32" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Building a half equation, one step at a time</text><text x="40" y="260" font-size="12">The electrons go on whichever side makes the two sides add up to the same charge.</text><text x="40" y="280" font-size="12">An atom losing electrons is oxidation; an ion gaining them is reduction.</text></g></svg>
caption: Four steps, in this order, every time.

md:
**The question.** Write the half equation for the change from an iron atom to an iron(III) ion.
**Step 1 — write the atom and the ion.** The (III) tells you the charge: $\ce{Fe -> Fe^{3+}}$.
**Step 2 — count the charge on each side.** Left: zero, because an atom is neutral. Right: +3. The two do not match, and they must.

prompt: How much charge has to be cancelled on the right-hand side?
explain: Three units of positive charge. Three electrons, each carrying one negative charge, will do it.

md:
**Step 3 — add electrons to the side that needs them.** The iron has *lost* three electrons, so they appear on the **right**, with the products: $\ce{Fe -> Fe^{3+} + 3e^-}$.
**Step 4 — check.** Left 0; right +3 and −3, which is 0. Balanced. And because electrons were lost, this half equation is an **oxidation**.

prompt: Now a reduction. Which is the half equation for a copper(II) ion becoming a copper atom?
explain: The ion gains two electrons, so they go in on the left with the reactants. Putting them on the right would make the charges +2 and −2, which do not match.

alt: Two labelled boxes joined by an arrow carrying two electrons: the reducing agent gives electrons away and is oxidised, the oxidising agent takes them and is reduced.
svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 296" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="cagt"><title id="cagt">Two boxes: the reducing agent gives electrons away and is itself oxidised, while the oxidising agent takes electrons and is itself reduced</title><defs><marker id="cag" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L10 5 L0 10 z" fill="currentColor"/></marker></defs><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.7"><rect x="40" y="90" width="270" height="110" rx="8"/><rect x="390" y="90" width="270" height="110" rx="8"/></g><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.4"><path d="M318 134 H382" marker-end="url(#cag)"/></g><g fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="1" stroke="none"><circle cx="336" cy="116" r="5"/><circle cx="356" cy="116" r="5"/></g><g font-family="inherit" font-size="13" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle"><text x="175" y="126" font-size="15" font-weight="600">reducing agent</text><text x="175" y="154">gives electrons away</text><text x="175" y="180">so it is oxidised itself</text><text x="525" y="126" font-size="15" font-weight="600">oxidising agent</text><text x="525" y="154">takes electrons</text><text x="525" y="180">so it is reduced itself</text><text x="350" y="104" font-size="11.5">electrons</text></g><g font-family="inherit" font-size="12.5" fill="currentColor"><text x="24" y="34" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Which one is the agent?</text><text x="24" y="54" font-size="11.5">The two filled circles on the arrow are electrons moving from left to right.</text><text x="24" y="240" font-size="11.5">In the blast furnace the carbon monoxide is the reducing agent: it takes the oxygen off the</text><text x="24" y="258" font-size="11.5">iron(III) oxide, and is itself oxidised to carbon dioxide while doing it.</text></g></svg>
caption: The agent is named for what it does to the other substance, not to itself.

md:
The **reducing agent** is the substance that reduces something else — so it gives its electrons (or takes the oxygen away), and is itself **oxidised**. The **oxidising agent** does the opposite: it takes electrons, so it is itself **reduced**.
The naming feels inside out until you read it as a job title. In the magnesium reaction, magnesium is the reducing agent and the copper(II) ions are the oxidising agent.

prompt: A substance gives its electrons away to another. What is it?
explain: It reduces the other substance by handing over electrons, and in doing so it is oxidised itself.

md:
Two industrial processes on this specification are redox from top to bottom.
In the **blast furnace**, carbon monoxide takes the oxygen from iron(III) oxide: $\ce{Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2}$. The iron(III) oxide is reduced; the carbon monoxide is oxidised; so **carbon monoxide is the reducing agent**.
In the **electrolysis of aluminium oxide**, $\ce{Al^{3+} + 3e^- -> Al}$ at the negative electrode is a reduction, and $\ce{2O^{2-} -> O2 + 4e^-}$ at the positive electrode is an oxidation.

title: GCSE Chemistry Revision "Oxidation and Reduction in Terms of Electrons"
why: A second pass over OIL RIG and half equations, with different examples from the ones above.

prompt: In the blast furnace, what is the reducing agent?
explain: Carbon monoxide takes the oxygen away from the iron(III) oxide, reducing it, and is itself oxidised to carbon dioxide.

md:
Define oxidation and reduction three ways: oxygen, hydrogen and electrons.
Say **which** substance in a given equation is oxidised and which is reduced.
Write a half equation and put the electrons on the correct side.
Name the oxidising agent and the reducing agent in a reaction.
Explain why the blast furnace and the aluminium cell are both redox.

Redox carries a whole C2 question most years, usually with rusting. A definition is **[1]**, and for reduction any one of the three will do. A half equation is **[3]**, awarded in a fixed order and each mark gated by the one above it, so a wrong formula costs all three. *Which species is oxidised* is **[1]**, and it wants the substance named, not a definition.
